title: CoreDNS cache tombstone buildup and long-tail query latency - scratchpad
short_summary: Working notes from triage of recurring p95/p99 DNS resolution latency caused by CoreDNS cache tombstone buildup. Includes timeline, evidence, short-term mitigations, and a draft runbook for on-call SREs.
body:
Background:

Starting late Oct 2024 we observed repeated p95/p99 DNS resolution latency spikes impacting API server-backed control plane calls and ingress readiness checks. Symptoms: elevated DNS latencies (~200-700ms p99), occasional NXDOMAINs for internal service names, and increased CPU/heap usage on CoreDNS pods. Impact: slow controller loops, delayed pod readiness, and sporadic 503s from frontend services.

Why this note exists: ongoing investigation shows a pattern consistent with CoreDNS cache tombstone (negative cache) entries accumulating in memory and not expiring quickly under certain forwarder behaviors. We don't have a full upstream fix yet; this doc collects evidence and a safer on-call runbook to mitigate without mass restarts.

Observed metrics / traces (key signals):
- prometheus: coredns_dns_request_duration_seconds{quantile=0.99} spikes correlate with coredns_process_resident_memory_bytes increases.
- coredns_cache_hits / cache_miss ratio dropped during spikes, with misses climbing.
- coredns_forward_errors and forward_request_total show intermittent DNS upstream timeouts coincident with increased tombstones.
- kube-apiserver dependent controllers (node/csr controllers) show increased reconcile latency in same windows.
- logs: repeated "servfail" and "read udp ...: i/o timeout" lines in CoreDNS logs when upstream forwarder transiently rate-limited.

Representative timeline (example incident 2024-10-28):
- 12:03 UTC: first p95 spike detected; tickets auto-created by alert rule SRE-DNS-P99.
- 12:08: on-call triage: confirmed CoreDNS p99 > 300ms, memory +50% vs baseline.
- 12:15: restart of single CoreDNS replica reduced p99 for ~10m then climbed again.
- 12:22: noticed increase in NXDOMAIN logs for stubDomain *.internal.company.local coming from upstream fallback.
- 12:40: scaling CoreDNS from 3->5 replicas reduced tail latencies for control-plane calls.
- 13:05: cluster-wide impact subsided after configuration change on upstream forwarder (reduced rate-limiting) + sticky local cache TTL bump.

Hypothesis (current):
- Under intermittent upstream errors (timeouts, SERVFAIL), CoreDNS's negative caching plugin (cache plugin storing tombstones for failed lookups) accumulates entries with TTLs that, under heavy churn and plugin interactions (forward -> cache -> kube-dns plugin), lead to a large in-memory index with stale tombstones. Those tombstones still get consulted causing increased processing time per query and GC pressure in Go runtime, which raises CPU/heap and increases qps latency.
- Subsequent cache misses and retries amplify when forwarders start rate-limiting, creating a feedback loop.

Evidence supporting hypothesis:
- Heap profiles show increased object counts associated with cache key structures and map overhead.
- Recreating upstream timeouts locally reproduces prolonged tail-latency window in a small test cluster.
- Restarting the coredns process (not whole deployment) returns memory to baseline immediately and reduces p99.

Short-term mitigation options (ordered by safety):
1) Sequential rolling restart of CoreDNS pods (one at a time) — low risk, but if tombstones rebuild quickly this is a short-lived fix. Use drain below.
2) Temporarily increase CoreDNS replicas to spread load and lower GC pressure per pod.
3) Adjust internal cache TTL for negative entries: reduce negative TTL in CoreDNS config (plugin cache: negative ttl) from 30s -> 5s as experiment in canary zone. Watch for increased upstream queries.
4) Upstream: request temporary rate-limit increase or smoothing for our forwarders to avoid transient SERVFAIL behavior.
5) If running older CoreDNS minor version, schedule upgrade to a release containing the cache bugfix (see linked GH PR).

Runbook (draft) - for on-call SREs:
Purpose: Mitigate control-plane and pod readiness impact from CoreDNS tombstone/cache buildup while minimizing blast radius.
Severity threshold: Alert SRE-DNS-P99 firing for >10m OR coredns_memory_resident > 1.5x baseline for >5m.

Immediate triage checklist:
- Who: oncall_sre, pager on rotation.
- Check cluster health and impact: kubectl get cs, kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o wide | grep coredns
- Grab metrics: curl -s http://prometheus.svc.cluster.local/api/v1/query?query=coredns_dns_request_duration_seconds{quantile=0.99} and check the last 1h.
- Logs: kubectl -n kube-system logs deploy/coredns -c coredns --since=30m | egrep "(servfail|i/o timeout|NXDOMAIN)"
- Memory/CPU: kubectl top pods -n kube-system | grep coredns.
- Check upstream health: ping/trace upstream resolver endpoints from a cluster node (dig @UPSTREAM +short <internal-record>) and inspect upstream rate-limiting headers if available.

Mitigation steps (safe order):
1) Scale CoreDNS up by +2 replicas: kubectl -n kube-system scale deployment/coredns --replicas=$(current+2). Wait 5-10m. Note: watch for kube-dns SRV hot-shots.
2) If scaling doesn't reduce p99, perform a sequential restart: for pod in $(kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=kube-dns -o name | shuf); do kubectl -n kube-system delete $pod --grace-period=30 --wait; sleep 60; check p99; done
   - Do NOT delete all pods at once. Check control-plane behavior between restarts.
3) If signal persists, apply a temporary configmap tweak to reduce negative cache TTL (example patch below). Apply to a single zone canary first.
4) Coordinate with infra team to check upstream resolvers and request smoothing or rate-limit adjustments.

Config change example (cache plugin snippet):
# existing: cache 30 {
#   success 3600
#   denial 30
# }
# experiment: lower negative caching TTL
cache 30 {
  success 3600
  denial 5
}

Notes on expected side effects: lower negative TTL increases upstream query rate for unresolved names; if upstream is the root cause (rate limiting) this can worsen short-term load. Always combine with upstream coordination or scaling.

Diagnostic commands collected:
- kubectl -n kube-system get deploy,coredns -o yaml
- kubectl -n kube-system exec -it deploy/coredns -- sh -c "cat /var/log/coredns.log | tail -n 200"
- curl http://localhost:9153/metrics | egrep "cache_hits|cache_miss|cache_ttl"
- pprof: kubectl -n kube-system port-forward deploy/coredns 6060:6060 &; go tool pprof http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/heap

Longer-term actions / follow-ups (owner assigned):
- SRE-4321: bake canary with reduced negative TTL and run for 72h to observe effect (owner: Marcus Lee).
- Upgrade CoreDNS to 1.11.x where cache-index memory leak patch is available (owner: Jordan Chen; PR link attached).
- Add a Prometheus alert for cache_miss / cache_hit ratio deviation and for high tombstone object growth (owner: Priya Raman).
- Investigate whether kube-dns plugin interactions (kubernetes plugin ordering) can be tuned to avoid expensive negative cache lookups for internal svc.cluster.local names.
- Postmortem draft if incident exceeds 4h of degraded p99: include timeline, root cause, mitigations, and follow-ups.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Are we seeing tombstones only for stubDomains or for all zones? (need log sampling).
- Does virtual node autoscaling behavior (autoscaler burst) interact with DNS query pattern to rebuild the cache faster?
- Can we route internal-lookup-only queries to a dedicated local resolver to reduce forwarder dependence?

Appendix: relevant snippets and links
- Prom query used: sum(rate(coredns_dns_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le) to reconstruct latency curve.
- Heap profile snapshots: s3://redwood-infra/sre/coredns/heap-2024-10-28-1200.pprof (private)
- Jira: https://redwood.atlassian.net/browse/SRE-4321
- GH PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/k8s-config/pull/987 (coredns config patch & canary change)

Notes to self: prioritize a non-disruptive canary test (reduce denial TTL in a single node pool) before touching upstream resolvers. Keep controller team in the loop if we hit readiness impacts.

End of scratchpad.
